body: Who was the founder of the **National Congress of British West Africa (NCBWA)**?
answer:
> [!answer]
> **J. E. Casely Hayford** of the Gold Coast, who founded it in **Accra in 1920** (with others such as Dr Akiwande Savage of Nigeria).
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The NCBWA united elites from the Gold Coast, Nigeria, Sierra Leone and the Gambia to demand **constitutional reforms** (elected representation, a West African university, an end to discrimination), an early form of regional nationalism. Casely Hayford also wrote _Ethiopia Unbound_ (1911).

## Simplified explanation

**J. E. Casely Hayford** founded the NCBWA in 1920.

body: Identify **two issues** that were discussed at the **Pan-African Conference in London in 1900**.
answer:
> [!answer]
> Any two: **racial discrimination** against Black people worldwide · the **treatment of Africans in South Africa** and Rhodesia (under Boer and British rule) · the **rights and self-government** of Africans in the colonies · an **appeal to Queen Victoria** and Western governments to protect African rights · Du Bois's declaration that **'the problem of the twentieth century is the problem of the colour line'**.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Organised by Trinidadian barrister **Henry Sylvester Williams** (Westminster Town Hall, July 1900), the conference gave the word 'Pan-African' currency; Du Bois drafted its 'Address to the Nations of the World'.

## Simplified explanation

The 1900 conference discussed **racism** and the **mistreatment of Africans in the colonies**, especially **South Africa**.

body: Why is **W. E. B. Du Bois** referred to as the **'Father of Pan-Africanism'**?
answer:
> [!answer]
> He **organised and led** the series of **Pan-African Congresses** (Paris 1919, London/Brussels/Paris 1921, London/Lisbon 1923, New York 1927) and **chaired the 1945 Manchester Congress**; he gave Pan-Africanism its **intellectual foundation** through his writings (_The Souls of Black Folk_, 1903) and the NAACP's journal **_The Crisis_**, which he edited; he championed the **rights and dignity of Black people** worldwide and later settled in **Ghana** (died in Accra, 1963).
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Du Bois' Pan-Africanism was **intellectual and reformist** (petitioning for colonial reform), contrasting with Garvey's **mass, separatist** 'Back to Africa' movement.

## Simplified explanation

Du Bois **organised the Pan-African Congresses** and **wrote** the ideas that inspired the movement.

body: Identify the **two main foci** of the newspapers **_The Negro World_** and **_The Crisis_**.
answer:
> [!answer]
> **_The Negro World_** (Marcus Garvey's UNIA): **racial pride and Black consciousness** ('Africa for the Africans'), **African redemption/Back to Africa** and Black economic self-reliance.
>
> **_The Crisis_** (W. E. B. Du Bois, NAACP): **civil rights and the fight against racial discrimination** (lynching, segregation), and the **intellectual and cultural achievements** of Black people.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Both papers circulated in Africa and the Caribbean (colonial authorities banned _The Negro World_ in several colonies), spreading Pan-African and anti-colonial ideas.

## Simplified explanation

Both papers promoted **Black pride** and fought **racial discrimination**; Garvey's also pushed **'Back to Africa'**.

body: Who was **Blaise Diagne**, and how significant was he to the genesis of the Pan-African movement in the 20th century?
answer:
> [!answer]
> **Blaise Diagne** (1872–1934) of **Senegal** was the **first Black African elected to the French National Assembly** (1914). He **helped Du Bois convene the First Pan-African Congress in Paris (1919)**, using his influence with French Prime Minister **Clemenceau** to obtain permission despite wartime restrictions, and **presided** over it.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Diagne also recruited West African soldiers (the tirailleurs sénégalais) for France in WWI in return for citizenship promises; his assimilationist stance later put him at odds with Garvey and radical Pan-Africanists.

## Simplified explanation

**Diagne**, a Senegalese French MP, **made the 1919 Paris Pan-African Congress possible** and chaired it.

answer:
> [!answer]
> **PAFMECA (Pan-African Freedom Movement of East and Central Africa):** formed in **Mwanza, Tanganyika, in 1958** (led by **Julius Nyerere**) to coordinate the **independence struggles** of nationalist movements in East and Central Africa.
>
> **PAFMECSA (Pan-African Freedom Movement of East, Central and Southern Africa):** PAFMECA **expanded in 1962** (Addis Ababa conference) to include **Southern African** liberation movements (e.g. the ANC, where Nelson Mandela spoke). It was **dissolved in 1963** when the **OAU** and its **Liberation Committee** took over its role.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

These regional bodies were precursors to continental unity, alongside the Casablanca and Monrovia groups, and helped build solidarity for decolonisation.

## Simplified explanation

**PAFMECA (1958)** coordinated freedom movements in **East and Central Africa**; it became **PAFMECSA (1962)** by adding **Southern Africa**, then merged into the **OAU** in 1963.

body: Identify and explain **two ideological differences** between the **Brazzaville (Monrovia) Group** and the **Casablanca Group**.
answer:
> [!answer]
> 1. **Approach to unity:** the **Casablanca Group** (Ghana, Guinea, Mali, Egypt, Morocco, Libya and the Algerian FLN) demanded **immediate political union**, a **continental government**; the **Monrovia/Brazzaville Group** (Nigeria, Liberia, Senegal, Côte d'Ivoire, Ethiopia and most francophone states) favoured **gradual, functional cooperation** (economic, cultural) while **preserving national sovereignty**.
> 2. **Ideological orientation and foreign relations:** Casablanca states were **radical, socialist-leaning and anti-imperialist**, supporting armed liberation (e.g. the Algerian FLN and Lumumba); Monrovia states were **moderate/conservative, pro-Western**, and close to former colonial powers (especially France).
> 3. **Non-interference:** Monrovia insisted on **non-interference in internal affairs** and **respect for colonial borders**, wary of Nkrumah's support for opposition movements.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The groups reconciled at the **Addis Ababa summit (May 1963)**, forming the OAU on the Monrovia group's largely functionalist terms.

## Simplified explanation

**Casablanca** wanted **one African government now** and was **radical**; **Monrovia** wanted **step-by-step cooperation**, kept **sovereignty** and was **pro-West**.

body: The **OAU Charter** made which city the headquarters of the OAU General Secretariat, and in which country is it located? Which city is the official administrative capital of the **African Union**?
answer:
> [!answer]
> **Addis Ababa, Ethiopia**, for both: the OAU Secretariat and today the **AU Commission** headquarters.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The OAU was founded in Addis Ababa on **25 May 1963** (now Africa Day) under Emperor Haile Selassie. Other AU organs are hosted elsewhere: the **Pan-African Parliament** (Midrand, South Africa) and the **African Court** (Arusha, Tanzania).

## Simplified explanation

**Addis Ababa, Ethiopia**.

body: Who was the **host and main convenor** of the OAU summit which produced the **Sirte Declaration**?
answer:
> [!answer]
> **Colonel Muammar Gaddafi** of **Libya**, who hosted the **Extraordinary OAU Summit at Sirte**, Libya, which adopted the **Sirte Declaration (9 September 1999)**, calling for the establishment of the **African Union**.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Gaddafi championed a 'United States of Africa'. The Constitutive Act was adopted at Lomé (2000) and the AU launched at Durban (July 2002).

## Simplified explanation

**Muammar Gaddafi** of **Libya**.

body: Identify **two objectives** of the AU as stated in the **Constitutive Act** of the Union. How many countries form the African Union?
answer:
> [!answer]
> **Objectives (Article 3; any two):** achieve **greater unity and solidarity** among African countries and peoples · **defend the sovereignty, territorial integrity and independence** of member states · **accelerate political and socio-economic integration** · promote **peace, security and stability** · promote **democratic principles, good governance and popular participation** · **promote and protect human and peoples' rights** · promote **sustainable development** · encourage international cooperation.
>
> **Membership:** **55** member states (all UN-recognised African states plus the Sahrawi Republic; Morocco rejoined in **2017**; it was 54 before then).
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Unlike the OAU, the AU's Act (Article 4(h)) allows **intervention** in grave circumstances (genocide, war crimes, crimes against humanity), shifting from 'non-interference' to 'non-indifference'.

## Simplified explanation

AU aims include **African unity**, **peace and security**, **integration**, **democracy** and **human rights**. It has **55** members.

body: Mention the name of **one Specialised Technical Committee** of the AU, and state **two** functions the **Assembly** of the AU has been mandated to perform.
answer:
> [!answer]
> **STCs (any one):** Agriculture, Rural Development, Water and Environment · Finance, Monetary Affairs, Economic Planning and Integration · Trade, Industry and Minerals · Transport, Infrastructure, Energy and Tourism · Health, Population and Drug Control · Education, Science and Technology · Defence, Safety and Security · Justice and Legal Affairs · Social Development, Labour and Employment.
>
> **Assembly functions (Article 9; any two):** **determine common policies** of the Union · **receive and decide on reports** of other organs · **consider requests for membership** · **establish organs** of the Union · **monitor implementation** of policies and decisions · **adopt the budget** · give **directives to the Executive Council** on conflicts, war and emergencies · **appoint the Chairperson** and Commissioners of the Commission (and the judges of the Court).
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The Assembly of Heads of State and Government is the AU's **supreme organ**, meeting at least once a year and deciding by consensus or a two-thirds majority.

## Simplified explanation

e.g. the **STC on Agriculture**. The Assembly **sets common policies** and **admits new members**.

body: State the **capital city** of each of the following countries: (a) Libya (b) the Democratic Republic of Congo (c) South Africa (d) Burkina Faso (e) Ethiopia.
answer:
> [!answer]
> (a) **Tripoli** · (b) **Kinshasa** · (c) **Pretoria** (executive; Cape Town is the legislative and Bloemfontein the judicial capital) · (d) **Ouagadougou** · (e) **Addis Ababa**.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Locations: Libya in North Africa; the DRC in Central Africa; South Africa at the continent's southern tip; Burkina Faso, landlocked in West Africa; Ethiopia in the Horn of Africa.

## Simplified explanation

**Tripoli, Kinshasa, Pretoria, Ouagadougou, Addis Ababa**.

body: Relate how the **OAU came into being**, provide reasons why it **gave way to the AU**, and explain **three reasons** why the OAU was a very significant creation in Africa.
answer:
**Formation:**
1. **Pan-African roots:** the Pan-African Congresses (1900–1945), especially Manchester 1945, and Nkrumah's 1958 **Conference of Independent African States** and **All-African People's Conference** in Accra.
2. **Rival blocs:** after 1960, the **Casablanca** (radical, immediate union) and **Monrovia/Brazzaville** (gradualist) groups divided independent states.
3. **Reconciliation:** Emperor **Haile Selassie** convened the **Addis Ababa summit**; on **25 May 1963**, 32 states signed the **OAU Charter**, a compromise favouring **sovereignty and functional cooperation**.

**Why it gave way to the AU:**
1. **Decolonisation was complete** (apartheid ended in 1994): the OAU's main purpose was achieved.
2. **Non-interference** (Article III) prevented action on **genocide (Rwanda 1994)**, civil wars, coups and dictatorships.
3. **Weak economic integration** and failure to address poverty and globalisation (the Lagos Plan and Abuja Treaty largely unimplemented).
4. **Institutional weaknesses:** no enforcement power, financial arrears, a 'dictators' club'.
5. **New vision:** the Sirte Declaration (1999), driven by Gaddafi, Mbeki and Obasanjo, called for a stronger union; the AU was launched in **Durban, 2002**.

**Significance of the OAU:**
1. **Liberation of Africa:** its **Liberation Committee** (Dar es Salaam) funded and supported liberation movements in Angola, Mozambique, Zimbabwe, Namibia and South Africa.
2. **Fight against apartheid:** it coordinated diplomatic isolation and sanctions against South Africa and Rhodesia.
3. **African unity and identity:** it gave Africa a **collective voice** at the UN and in world affairs, and promoted solidarity.
4. **Border stability:** the 1964 Cairo resolution on **respect for colonial borders** reduced inter-state wars.
5. **Conflict mediation:** in some disputes (Algeria–Morocco 1963), and it established foundations for later African institutions (the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights, 1981; the African Development Bank).

> [!answer]
> Formation: Pan-African roots, the Casablanca vs Monrovia rivalry, reconciled at Addis Ababa (25 May 1963). Transition to the AU: decolonisation complete, non-interference failures (Rwanda), weak economic integration, institutional weaknesses, the Sirte vision leading to Durban 2002. Significance: liberation support, the anti-apartheid struggle, a collective African voice, border stability, mediation and institution-building.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The OAU is often judged a success at decolonisation but a failure at governance and integration. The AU's Constitutive Act introduced the Peace and Security Council, the Pan-African Parliament and the right of intervention.

## Simplified explanation

The OAU was formed in **1963** when rival African groups agreed to unite. It **helped free Africa** and **fight apartheid**, but it **couldn't stop wars and dictators**, so it became the **AU in 2002**.

body: Briefly explain how **Marcus Garvey** and **Kwame Nkrumah** inspired the Pan-African movement and anti-colonial sentiments in the **African diaspora** and **Africa** respectively.
answer:
**Marcus Garvey (1887–1940), the diaspora:**
1. Founded the **Universal Negro Improvement Association (UNIA)** in Jamaica (1914), later based in Harlem, New York, with millions of followers: the largest Black mass movement of its time.
2. Preached **racial pride**, **Black self-reliance** and **'Africa for the Africans, at home and abroad'**.
3. Launched the **Back to Africa** movement and the **Black Star Line** shipping company (1919) to link Black people economically.
4. Spread ideas through the **_Negro World_** newspaper, circulated across the Caribbean, the US and Africa (and banned by colonial governments).
5. Inspired later leaders (Nkrumah called Garvey's writings the most influential on him; Ghana's **Black Star** emblem honours him).

**Kwame Nkrumah (1909–1972), Africa:**
1. Co-organised the **1945 Manchester Pan-African Congress**, shifting the movement to Africa and demanding immediate independence.
2. Led the **Gold Coast to independence (6 March 1957)** as the first sub-Saharan colony, a beacon for others: 'Our independence is meaningless unless it is linked up with the total liberation of Africa.'
3. Hosted the **Conference of Independent African States** and the **All-African People's Conference (1958)** in Accra, uniting nationalists (Lumumba, Kenyatta's associates, Banda).
4. Supported liberation movements (training, funding, the Bureau of African Affairs).
5. Championed **continental union** (_Africa Must Unite_, 1963) and was a founding father of the **OAU**; wrote against neo-colonialism.

> [!answer]
> Garvey: the UNIA, racial pride, 'Africa for the Africans', Back to Africa and the Black Star Line, the Negro World, inspiration for later leaders. Nkrumah: Manchester 1945, Ghana's independence as a beacon, the 1958 Accra conferences, support for liberation movements, advocacy of continental union and the OAU, anti-neo-colonialism writings.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Garvey's mass, populist Pan-Africanism contrasted with Du Bois' intellectual approach; Nkrumah fused Pan-Africanism with nationalism and socialism, making Accra the 'Mecca' of African liberation in the late 1950s.

## Simplified explanation

**Garvey** gave Black people in the diaspora **pride and hope** ('Africa for the Africans'). **Nkrumah** won **Ghana's independence**, hosted **African conferences** and pushed for **African unity**.
hint: Garvey: mass diaspora movement; Nkrumah: continental leadership.

body: Compare the nationalist struggles (pro-independence agitations) of the **Gold Coast** and **Kenya** from the 1940s onwards, and explain how the colonial regimes in those countries shaped the form and nature of each struggle.
answer:
**Gold Coast (largely constitutional, non-violent):**
- **1948 riots** (the ex-servicemen's march and Christiansborg shooting; boycotts) led to the **Watson Commission** and the **Coussey Committee**.
- The **UGCC** (1947) and the more radical **CPP** (1949) under Nkrumah demanded 'Self-Government Now'.
- **Positive Action** (1950): strikes, boycotts and non-violent resistance; Nkrumah was jailed, then won the **1951 elections** and became Leader of Government Business.
- Progressive constitutional advance: elections in 1954 and 1956, then **independence on 6 March 1957**.

**Kenya (largely armed):**
- The **KAU** (Kenya African Union) under **Jomo Kenyatta** sought land and political reforms, but was blocked.
- **Mau Mau (Land and Freedom Army)** rebellion (1952–60), mainly Kikuyu, fought for land and freedom; the British declared a **State of Emergency** (1952), detained tens of thousands in camps, and killed over 11,000 rebels; Kenyatta was imprisoned (the Kapenguria trial).
- After the Emergency, constitutional talks (the **Lancaster House conferences**, 1960, 1962), KANU and KADU, and **independence on 12 December 1963**.

**How colonial regimes shaped the struggles:**
1. **Settler presence:** the Gold Coast had **no significant white settler population**, so Britain had less to protect and was willing to negotiate; Kenya's **powerful white settlers** in the **White Highlands** resisted African advancement, making peaceful change difficult and provoking armed revolt.
2. **Land alienation:** Kenyan Africans (especially the Kikuyu) lost fertile land to settlers, creating deep grievances; in the Gold Coast, land largely remained in African hands (cocoa farming).
3. **Colonial policy and repression:** British authorities in the Gold Coast responded to unrest with **commissions and constitutional reforms**; in Kenya, they used **repression** (Emergency laws, detention camps), radicalising the struggle.
4. **Indirect rule and African elites:** the Gold Coast's educated elite and chiefs participated in legislative councils (since 1925); Kenya's African political participation was very limited.

**Similarities:** both were British colonies; both had post-war grievances (ex-servicemen, economic hardship); both leaders (Nkrumah and Kenyatta) were jailed and then became heads of government.

> [!answer]
> Gold Coast: the 1948 riots, the Watson and Coussey reforms, the UGCC and CPP, Positive Action, the 1951 elections, gradual constitutional advance to 1957 (non-violent). Kenya: KAU frustration, the Mau Mau armed revolt (1952–60), the State of Emergency and detention, Lancaster House, independence in 1963. Shaping factors: settler absence vs a powerful settler presence, land alienation, reform vs repression, the degree of African participation. Similarities: post-war grievances, jailed leaders becoming heads of government.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The contrast illustrates the 'settler colony' vs 'non-settler colony' distinction in decolonisation studies (e.g. Algeria, Rhodesia and Kenya vs the Gold Coast and Nigeria). Recent scholarship (Caroline Elkins, _Imperial Reckoning_) documents British abuses during Kenya's Emergency; the UK compensated Mau Mau victims in 2013.

## Simplified explanation

The **Gold Coast** won independence **peacefully** through **parties, strikes and elections**, as there were **few white settlers**. **Kenya** had many **white settlers who took land**, so Africans fought the **Mau Mau war** before winning independence.
hint: Describe each, then link to colonial context.

body: Discuss **four challenges** of the **African Union** and propose remedies for these challenges.
answer:
1. **Funding and dependence on external donors:** a large share of the AU budget (especially peace operations) has come from **foreign partners** (the EU, China, the US), undermining autonomy; many members are in arrears.
   - _Remedy:_ implement the **Kigali financing decision (2016)**: a **0.2% import levy** on eligible imports; sanctions for arrears; a fully funded **Peace Fund**.
2. **Insecurity and conflicts:** terrorism (al-Shabaab, Boko Haram, Sahel jihadists), civil wars (Sudan, South Sudan, Ethiopia's Tigray, the DRC), and a **resurgence of coups** (Mali, Guinea, Burkina Faso, Niger, Gabon).
   - _Remedy:_ operationalise the **African Standby Force** and early-warning system; consistent sanctions against coups; address root causes (governance, poverty, youth unemployment).
3. **Weak enforcement and lack of political will:** decisions and treaties are poorly implemented; **sovereignty concerns** limit action; leaders shield each other (the 'non-indifference' principle under-used).
   - _Remedy:_ binding compliance mechanisms; strengthen the **African Court** and the **APRM**; empower the **Pan-African Parliament** with legislative powers.
4. **Bad governance and democratic backsliding:** term-limit manipulation, rigged elections, human rights abuses.
   - _Remedy:_ enforce the **African Charter on Democracy, Elections and Governance**; credible election observation; support civil society.
5. **Slow economic integration:** overlapping RECs, poor infrastructure and non-tariff barriers hinder the **AfCFTA**.
   - _Remedy:_ harmonise RECs, invest in infrastructure (PIDA), implement AfCFTA protocols and free movement.
6. **External interference** and divided loyalties to former colonial powers or new partners.
   - _Remedy:_ common African positions (the Common African Position), self-reliance and Agenda 2063.

> [!answer]
> Challenges: donor dependence and arrears (remedy: the Kigali import levy and a funded Peace Fund); conflicts, terrorism and coups (the Standby Force, early warning, consistent sanctions, root causes); weak enforcement and political will (binding compliance, a stronger Court, APRM and PAP); bad governance (enforce ACDEG, observation, civil society); slow integration (harmonise RECs, PIDA, AfCFTA, free movement); external interference (common positions, Agenda 2063).
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The **Kagame reform report (2017)** proposed institutional reforms (focused priorities, a leaner Commission, financial self-reliance). Agenda 2063 sets the long-term vision; the AU joined the **G20** as a permanent member in 2023.

## Simplified explanation

The AU struggles with **too little money**, **wars and coups**, **weak enforcement** and **bad governance**. Fix it with **self-funding**, a **ready peace force**, **binding rules** and **support for democracy**.
hint: Four challenges, each with a concrete remedy.
